quote: Wie viel Lagen können $n$ Kreise in der Ebene annehmen?
english: How many configurations can n circles in the plane assume?
topic: Three short notes: questions on the discriminant of a quadratic form built from the roots of an algebraic equation (the equation with real roots in lambda), a question on directly proving regularity of solutions of differential equations other than Laplace's, and the problem of counting the possible configurations of n circles in the plane.

triage.modern_statement: Hilbert left the question unspecified, so this is a modern reading of it. Classify the arrangements of n circles in the real (affine) plane up to topological or combinatorial equivalence, and count them as a function of n. One standard version: count arrangements in general position (no three circles through one point, tangencies handled under a fixed convention) where two arrangements count as the same if one can be deformed continuously into the other, keeping every circle circular, without changing the intersection pattern. A related question asks which combinatorial arrangements of pseudocircles can actually be drawn with true circles ('circularizability'). If Hilbert meant only circles that do not cross, the configurations are just nestings. That simpler count is a classical rooted-tree enumeration, but I did not confirm it with a source here.
triage.answered_by: Hilbert's notebook question is not on record as answered, and no general formula is known. Small cases have been counted under the modern definition in OEIS A250001 (proposed by Jonathan Wild, with Christopher Jones working on n=5): 1, 1, 3, 14, 173, 16951 for n = 0..5. Felsner and Scheucher (arXiv 1712.02149) used computers to list arrangements of up to 6 or 7 pseudocircles, worked out which arrangements with 5 or 6 pseudocircles can be drawn with true circles, and gave asymptotic bounds.

evidence.claim: OEIS A250001, 'Number of arrangements of n circles in the affine plane', gives the terms 1, 1, 3, 14, 173, 16951. Its definition: no three circles meet at a point, and two arrangements count as the same if one can be deformed continuously into the other while the circles stay circular and the intersection pattern does not change.

The A250001 comments say that from n=5 on, geometry rules out some topologically possible arrangements: 16977 arrangements of 5 pseudocircles were enumerated, but not all of them can be drawn with real circles.
Sloane's 2018 article in the AMS Notices discusses A250001 ('circles in the plane'), which was runner-up in an OEIS vote for favourite sequence.

Felsner and Scheucher used computers to generate all connected arrangements of n≤6 pseudocircles and all intersecting arrangements of n≤7. They classified which ones can be drawn with circles and gave asymptotic results on how many arrangements there are.
A 2025 arXiv paper still cites A250001 as an open-ended enumeration problem and points to a recent survey of related sequences.

triage.why: The note is a single sentence with no definition of 'Lage' (configuration), so it is hard to say exactly which equivalence Hilbert intended. Under the natural modern reading, counting topologically distinct arrangements of n circles in the plane, the problem is well known. Exact counts exist only up to n=5, no closed formula is known, and work on pseudocircle arrangements and circularizability is ongoing (2017 to 2025 papers). It is not one of Hilbert's 23 problems or the 24th. It resembles the topological question in the first part of his 16th problem (how ovals can be arranged), but I found no source that links this notebook entry to that problem. I also found no evidence that Hilbert or anyone else answered this specific question.
